# Three Phases of Normal Recovery: On-Going, Rapid and Delayed (Zalessky, 1979)

**What it is** — Near the opening of 8.6 the authors write: "Restoration is based upon the awareness that three fairly discrete phases of the normal recovery process may be distinguished (Zalessky, 1979):" "*On-going recovery*, which takes place during the activity itself"; "*Rapid recovery*, which occurs immediately after exercise, leading to removal of metabolic by-products and replenishment of depleted energy resources"; and "*Delayed recovery*, which surpasses the initial level if training loads are not excessive" (PDF 455 / p.444, checked against the page image; italics in the original).

**Why it works** — The authors give the phases as the base that restoration rests on, without a separate mechanism. Inference: the three phases separate what restoration can target. On-going recovery happens inside the work (between efforts), rapid recovery is the clearing and refuelling just after it, and delayed recovery is where the rise above baseline happens. The later 8.6 material leans on this split: recovery is fastest "immediately upon cessation of exercise, after which it diminishes gradually," so it is "more advisable to accelerate recovery processes when their natural rate is slowing down" (Talyshev, 1977; PDF 462 / p.451).

**When to apply** — When deciding what a restorative means is for. A means used between efforts serves on-going recovery; one used straight after the session serves rapid recovery; and the delayed phase is the one to protect if the goal is adaptation rather than readiness for the next bout. Inference: this is the frame behind the timing rule in [[heuristic--time-restoration-to-when-work-capacity-is-next-needed]] and the blunting warning in [[heuristic--routine-artificial-restoration-can-blunt-adaptation]].

**When NOT to apply** — Zalessky (1979) is cited for a classification only; no study design, measures or durations are given, so `untested`. The phases have no time boundaries on the page, so they cannot be used to schedule a session by the clock. The delayed phase carries its own condition: it "surpasses the initial level if training loads are not excessive," so the frame does not promise supercompensation after any load. "Fairly discrete" is the book's own hedge; the phases overlap in practice.

**Example** — The Talyshev timing study in the same section reads well through this frame: sauna and hydrotherapy straight after the workout (rapid phase) helped that day but left next-day work capacity below its initial level, while the same therapy 6-9 hours later produced next-day supercompensation (PDF 462 / p.451). See [[case-study--talyshev-sauna-and-hydrotherapy-timing-0-3-6-9-hours]].

**Related** — [[claim--deeper-workout-fatigue-gives-larger-after-effects-if-loads-are-carefully-prescribed]], [[heuristic--incomplete-restoration-workouts-zalessky-rules]], [[framework--restoration-times-by-biochemical-process-table-2]] (9.1, timing by process), [[principle--restoration-is-part-of-training-and-distinct-from-rehabilitation]]

# Exercise Safety Comes Mainly From Skill, Built by Progressing Carefully on Nine Factors

**What it is** — The closing rule of 8.8: "In general, exercise safety is largely a consequence of skill development (neuromuscular efficiency) and may be enhanced by imposing activities which progress carefully with respect to factors such as complexity, intensity, volume, speed, range of movement, duration, variety, level of fatigue and mental state" (PDF 478 / p.467, checked against the page image). The page names nine factors, and "such as" marks the list as open.

**Why it works** — The authors' mechanism is in the parenthesis: skill is "neuromuscular efficiency," so a skilled athlete controls the load and the body's position under it. Inference: this ties the section's opening rule, "There is no such thing as a dangerous exercise .... There is only a dangerous way of doing any exercise" (PDF 471 / p.460), to a method. If danger lies in the way an exercise is done, safety is built by improving the way, and the nine factors are the dials that let an athlete meet a harder version only after mastering an easier one. The sentence just before it on the same page gives the extreme case: Russian weightlifters "holding a snatch overhead in the low squat position and shifting in different directions to move the bar into unstable positions which they are then compelled to control by astute postural adjustments" (PDF 478 / p.467).

**When to apply** — When an exercise is judged risky for an athlete: before dropping it, ask which of the nine factors can be lowered so the athlete can do it well, then raise them one at a time. Fatigue and mental state are on the list, so the same lift can be safe fresh and unsafe at the end of a hard session or under stress. Inference: this fits a return-to-training progression, where complexity, speed and range are often raised in a set order.

**When NOT to apply** — The rule is the authors' summary, with no study or progression rates, so `untested`. "Largely" leaves room for causes skill cannot remove: the same section lists accidents, cumulative overload and individual responses among injury causes (PDF 471 / p.460), and says injury "can be minimised, but not entirely prevented." The list gives no order for which factor to raise first. Inference: skill does not protect tissue that has not adapted to the load; the 8.8 overuse material still applies to a skilled athlete.

**Example** — The authors' own: the snatch-shifting drill above trains a weightlifter to recover a bar that drifts out of position, which raises complexity and variety on purpose once the basic lift is secure (PDF 478 / p.467). See [[heuristic--imperfection-training-practise-imperfect-execution-and-contingency-actions]].

**Related** — [[framework--no-dangerous-exercises-rule-and-its-eight-qualifications]], [[framework--six-fundamental-principles-of-the-injury-process]], [[heuristic--progress-skills-only-at-70-80-percent-technical-reliability]], [[principle--prepare-athletes-for-risky-movements-instead-of-avoiding-them]], [[heuristic--program-variable-complexity-scales-with-training-age]]

# Run Short Hills at a Low Rate With a Forward Take-Off and Active Leg Swing; Half-Bent "Dribbling" Legs Ruin the Exercise

**What it is** — In 9.2, item 7 of Verkhoshansky's program for perfecting starting acceleration: "Uphill running (15-25 m.) should be executed at a low rate with emphasis on a forward take-off and active swing movements of the leg. Running with half bent legs like dribbling is a huge mistake: it lowers the specificity of the training influence of this exercise" (PDF 584 / p.573, checked against the page image). 9.2 is written in the first person by Dr. Yuri Verkhoshansky.

**Why it works** — His stated reason is specificity: the half-bent, short-stepping pattern "lowers the specificity of the training influence." Inference: the program's target is the push-off of the starting acceleration, so each uphill stride should be a full forward take-off with a driven swing leg. A low stride rate leaves time for that full extension on each step, while quick, flexed-knee steps turn the drill into fast shuffling that resembles neither the start nor the bounding work beside it in the program.

**When to apply** — When short hill runs (15-25 m) are used to build starting acceleration in sprinters or other speed-strength athletes. Cue a forward take-off, an active swing of the leg and a low stride rate, and stop the rep if the athlete starts to run with half-bent legs. In Verkhoshansky's program the hills come alongside heavy squats, loaded jumps, depth jumps, multiple bounds and stadium jumps (PDF 583-584 / pp.572-573).

**When NOT to apply** — The cue is one sentence of his program, with no test of the technique itself, so `untested`. It is given for 15-25 m hills inside a starting-acceleration block; it does not cover longer hill runs for conditioning or steep grades, and the page gives no gradient. Inference: "low rate" means stride frequency, not low effort; the page does not say the runs are submaximal. The program is meant for prepared athletes, and the depth jumps in it are shock-method work, which Verkhoshansky restricts in the same section to experienced athletes (see [[principle--reserve-the-shock-method-for-experienced-top-level-athletes-not-youth]]).

**Example** — The program's own list puts the cue beside the other jump means: stadium jumps "executed with 2-3 steps at a time with an active take-off in an upward and forward direction," then uphill running with the forward take-off cue (PDF 584 / p.573). Both drills ask for the same thing: an active, forward-directed take-off on each contact.

**Related** — [[case-study--six-week-starting-acceleration-program-squats-loaded-jumps-depth-jumps-bounds-hills]], [[case-study--alternate-leg-bounding-with-thigh-cuffs-for-sprinters]], [[heuristic--cue-maximal-jump-height-not-knee-angle-and-fix-depth-with-plinths]], [[principle--accelerating-specific-adaptation]]

# Talyshev: Sauna Plus Hydrotherapy Right After a Workout Helped That Day but Hurt the Next; 6-9 Hours Later It Produced Supercompensation

**What it is** — Talyshev (1977) "conducted research on a large group of highly qualified athletes who followed a standardised training programme. Following a workout, the athletes took a sauna in combination with hydrotherapy - in one case directly after the workout; in the other cases, 3, 6, and 9 hours later, accompanied by a large battery of physiological tests" (PDF 462 / p.451, checked against the page image). Results as reported:
- No baths or hydrotherapy: work capacity "dropped sharply immediately after the workout," and "noticeable recovery commenced on the following day."
- Immediately after: "a marked increase in work capacity immediately following the therapy and 3 hours later. However, this increase slowed down, and work capacity did not recover and even fell below its initial level on the following day."
- At 3 hours: "a pronounced increase in work capacity 6 hours after the therapy (9 hours after the workout). Work capacity returned to its initial level on the following day."
- At 6, "and especially 9 hours": "work capacity not only recovered on the following day, but there was significant increase (supercompensation)" (PDF 462 / p.451).

**Why it works** — The setup in the book: "The highest intensity and rate of recovery is observed immediately upon cessation of exercise, after which it diminishes gradually (Talyshev, 1977). Logically, *it is more advisable to accelerate recovery processes when their natural rate is slowing down*" (PDF 462, italics in the original). The book frames recovery in three phases (Zalessky, 1979): "On-going recovery" during activity; "Rapid recovery" immediately after, "leading to removal of metabolic by-products and replenishment of depleted energy resources"; and "Delayed recovery, which surpasses the initial level if training loads are not excessive" (PDF 455 / p.444). Inference: an intervention during the rapid phase adds little to a process already running fast and may cut short the signal; one in the delayed phase supports the process when it slows.

**When to apply** — As evidence for timing heat and water therapies by the next performance demand, not by habit (see [[heuristic--time-restoration-to-when-work-capacity-is-next-needed]]).

**When NOT to apply** — The book gives no sample size, no measure of "work capacity," no statistics and no control for the order of conditions; "large group of highly qualified athletes" is all that is said. The result is for sauna plus hydrotherapy; it says nothing on its own about massage, cold or compression. The "no therapy" condition is described only qualitatively, so the supercompensation at 6-9 hours is not compared numerically with it.

**Example** — The study's sharpest contrast: therapy straight after the workout left next-day work capacity "below its initial level," while the same therapy 9 hours later produced next-day "significant increase (supercompensation)" (PDF 462 / p.451).

**Related** — [[heuristic--time-restoration-to-when-work-capacity-is-next-needed]], [[heuristic--routine-artificial-restoration-can-blunt-adaptation]], [[claim--adaptive-reconstruction-vs-supercompensation]], [[research-papers/dupuy-2018-an-evidence-based-approach-for-choosing-post-exercise-recovery-techniques-to-reduce-marker]]. From 9.1: [[claim--clearing-metabolites-during-rest-blunts-adaptive-protein-synthesis]] (9.1: metabolite dispersal during rest "in principle, not expedient"; rated contested against the 6-9 hour result here).

# "No Dangerous Exercise, Only a Dangerous Way of Doing It": the Rule and the Eight Facts That Limit It

**What it is** — Section 8.8 restates an earlier rule and then qualifies it: "At the very outset, let us reiterate what has been said before: There is no such thing as a dangerous exercise .... There is only a dangerous way of doing any exercise. Is this a valid general rule? While it is very often true, we also have to note that:" (PDF 471 / p.460, checked against the page image; "exercise" and "true" sit on the compressed right margin and are partly reconstructed). The eight qualifications: "Injury is often a cumulative process"; "The most recent exercise or activity can be the final trigger"; "Injuries may be the result of "too much, too soon" of a safe thing (overtraining)"; "Injuries may be caused by inadequate pre-exercise preparation ("warm-up")"; "Accidents happen"; "Cause and effect are not linearly related"; "Individual responses to exercise are different"; "Injuries are context or situation dependent" (PDF 471 / p.460). Later the authors add that "Many manoeuvres which necessitate a high degree of skill or courage should undoubtedly be labelled as intrinsically dangerous for the average person, but not for the expert performer. There are safe and dangerous ways of executing virtually every human movement, including sitting, standing and walking" (PDF 472 / p.461). On PDF 477 they restate it: "the lack of safety in exercise is not simply a consequence of so-called dangerous exercises, but also one of unsafe execution of any exercise. Exercise safety must always be viewed in the context of the overall training session or programme for each specific individual" (PDF 477 / p.466, partly reconstructed at the right margin: "lack of", "execution of", "programme").

**Why it works** — The authors' reasoning: risk is a property of the exercise, the person, their state and the whole programme together. "While certain exercises may be intrinsically less safe for the relative novice to training, they may pose minimal risks for the same person after several months of training. Conversely, the least demanding and simplest of exercises may cause serious injury to an elite athlete who is careless, unmotivated or overtrained" (PDF 477 / p.466). The section closes: "exercise safety is largely a consequence of skill development (neuromuscular efficiency) and may be enhanced by imposing activities which progress carefully with respect to factors such as complexity, intensity, volume, speed, range of movement, duration, variety, level of fatigue and mental state" (PDF 478 / p.467).

**When to apply** — When someone wants an exercise banned as "dangerous": ask for whom, in what state, at what dose and inside what programme. For beginners the authors still say "it is undoubtedly preferable to err on the side of conservatism," while warning that "religious avoidance of certain exercises can lead to an overall imbalance between muscle groups or in motor coordination and increase the likelihood of injury during the sports event. Furthermore, the avoidance of exercising a muscle group in a particular way never enhances safety; it simply weakens those muscles relative to the exercise pattern which is avoided" (PDF 477 / p.466). Eric's review: "safety first, keep things simple, teach basic movement skills and basic lifts before anything advanced, treat strength as the base, and require bodyweight competency before loaded work." (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 41, Inferred (transcript + Week 1 slides)). Inference: that is the authors' "err on the side of conservatism" for beginners, paired with their progression rule rather than a ban.

**When NOT to apply** — The rule is the authors' position, not a tested finding; no injury data are given, so `untested`. Their own list says the rule fails where injury is cumulative, nonlinear or triggered by "too much, too soon" of a safe exercise, so it is not a licence to load anything well executed. "Never enhances safety" is an absolute with no evidence behind it. Inference: in rehabilitation, holding back a loading pattern for a time is standard graded exposure, not the "religious avoidance" the authors criticise.

**Example** — The authors' own: a demanding exercise that is "intrinsically less safe for the relative novice" may "pose minimal risks for the same person after several months of training" (PDF 477 / p.466).

**Related** — [[heuristic--no-unsafe-stretch-only-unsafe-execution-for-individual]] (the same rule for stretching, 3.5.6), [[principle--prepare-athletes-for-risky-movements-instead-of-avoiding-them]] (8.2), [[framework--six-fundamental-principles-of-the-injury-process]], [[heuristic--imperfection-training-practise-imperfect-execution-and-contingency-actions]]

# Verkhoshansky's 6-Week Starting-Acceleration Program: Squats, Loaded and Kettlebell Jumps, Depth Jumps, Multiple Bounds, Stadium Jumps and Short Hills

**What it is** — "Program for Perfecting Starting Acceleration" (PDF 583-586 / pp.572-575; numbers read from the page images, since the table OCR scrambles the rows). It "is executed two times a week for six weeks for a total of 12 training sessions" with seven means (PDF 583-584):
1. Barbell squats at "80-90% of maximum for development of maximum strength and for toning the central nervous system".
2. Vertical jumps with the bar on the shoulders (Fig 21) "using a weight of 30-50% of maximum", for explosive strength.
3. Kettlebell squat jumps (Fig 22), 16, 24 or 32 kg "chosen depending upon the athlete", for reactive ability; a dumbbell will do if no kettlebell is available.
4. Depth jumps, for explosive strength and reactive ability.
5. Six-fold and ten-fold "leg-to-leg bounds from place executed with maximum effort", for "repeated explosive effort and anaerobic capacity".
6. Stadium jumps up stairs, "for development of maximal anaerobic capacity", "2-3 steps at a time with an active take-off in an upward and forward direction".
7. Uphill running, 15-25 m, "at a low rate with emphasis on a forward take-off and active swing movements of the leg. Running with half bent legs like dribbling is a huge mistake: it lowers the specificity of the training influence of this exercise."

The sessions: 1, 2 and 4 are squats only (85-90% 2-3 x 5-6; then pyramids); 3 and 7 pair bar jumps with six-fold bounds; 5 pairs depth jumps (0.75 m, 2 x 10 per series) with ten-fold bounds, with the series repeated 2-3 times (PDF 585 / p.574; Inference: 40-60 depth jumps in the session); 6 pairs kettlebell squat jumps 3 x 8 with ten-fold bounds; 7, 9 and 11 end with uphill runs 1 x 5-6 after 15 min rest; 8, 10 and 12 are depth jumps 4 x 10 (0.75 m in session 8, 1.10 m in 10 and 12) then stadium jumps 4 x 10 in 2-3 series; 9 and 11 pair squats at 93-95% 2 x 2-3 with depth jumps from 1.10 m, 2 x 10 (PDF 584-586 / pp.573-575). Rests are long: 4-6 min between sets and 8-12 min between series.

**Recorded as printed (Inference: likely errors):** the exercise list gives the bar jumps at "30-50% of maximum" (PDF 583), but sessions 3 and 7 prescribe "Vertical jumps with bar (50-60%)" (PDF 584-585). Session 2 gives "(93-95%)" for "1 x 12" (PDF 584 / p.573), while the same pyramid in the leg program puts 1 x 2 at the top load (PDF 579 / p.568). The book does not reconcile either.

**Why it works** — His stated purposes are per means (list above): maximal strength and CNS "toning" from squats, explosive strength from loaded jumps, reactive ability from kettlebell and depth jumps, repeated explosive effort and anaerobic capacity from bounds and stairs, and a specific forward take-off from hills. Inference: the program moves from mostly squats (sessions 1-4) toward depth jumps, stairs and hills (sessions 8-12), the same rising specificity as the leg program. Inference: sessions 9 and 11 pair squats at 93-95% 2 x 2-3 with depth jumps from 1.10 m 2 x 10 in one series (PDF 585-586 / pp.574-575), a heavy-then-explosive complex of the kind the book calls the after-effect in 3.4.2 ([[framework--post-activation-potentiation-load-timing-sequencing]]); the squats are listed "for toning the central nervous system" (PDF 583 / p.572), but he gives no reason for the pairing.

**When to apply** — Inference: a short pre-season block for athletes whose event starts from rest (sprint starts, football get-off), who already squat and jump. The hill cue is concrete: forward take-off and active leg swing, not a shuffling, bent-leg run. Eric's baseline: "0-10m is read as an acceleration score (reflecting maximal strength/power/slow stretch-shortening-cycle development)" (`docs/method-baseline.md` line 94, Legacy (interview 2026-09-28, Q8)). Inference: that reading matches his mix of heavy squats and loaded jumps for starting acceleration; a 0-10 m split before and after the six weeks would test it.

**When NOT to apply** — No outcome data, sport, level or test is given. Stadium jumps and bounds are aimed at "anaerobic capacity"; Inference: that is not a starting-acceleration quality; they serve repeat-effort ability, and could be cut for an athlete who only needs single starts. Depth jumps from 1.10 m in four sessions limit this to athletes who meet his "experienced top level" condition ([[principle--reserve-the-shock-method-for-experienced-top-level-athletes-not-youth]]). Do not quote the bar-jump load without the 30-50% and 50-60% conflict. Session 5 can total 60 depth jumps when its series is repeated three times (PDF 585 / p.574). That exceeds the 4 x 10 session cap in item 2 (PDF 577 / p.566). The text gives no exception for this program.

**Example** — Session 9: squats at 93-95% 2 x 2-3 paired with depth jumps from 1.10 m 2 x 10, the pair repeated twice with 10-12 min between series; then 15 min rest and 5-6 uphill runs of 15-25 m with 4-6 min between (PDF 585 / p.574).

**Related** — [[heuristic--cue-maximal-jump-height-not-knee-angle-and-fix-depth-with-plinths]] (footnotes 26-27 on the two loaded jumps); [[case-study--twelve-week-leg-program-squats-then-barbell-jumps-then-depth-and-box-jumps]]; [[claim--absolute-leg-strength-connects-to-sprint-speed-only-indirectly-via-jump]]; [[claim--optimal-depth-jump-drop-height-for-power-vs-force]]; [[heuristic--cyclic-vs-acyclic-speed-strength-tempo-rest-and-fatigue]]; [[framework--post-activation-potentiation-load-timing-sequencing]] (3.4.2, the after-effect; the squat + depth jump series in sessions 9 and 11); [[case-study--junior-sprinters-short-and-long-jump-training-effects]] (5.3, the "short jumps" class, repeated standing multi-jumps such as the six-fold and ten-fold bounds here, which there "developed primarily length and speed of the running stride"); [[case-study--alternate-leg-bounding-with-thigh-cuffs-for-sprinters]] (5.2.3, leg-to-leg bounding over 50-100 m, the long form)

# Endurance Training Builds Mitochondrial Protein in Both Slow and Fast Fibres, Without Skeletal-Muscle Hypertrophy

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky (9.1 §1.4, PDF 528-529 / p.517-518, checked against the page images): "training for endurance is not combined with general hypertrophy of the skeletal muscles and an increase in the myofibril mass. In place of this, there is a small increase in the cell cytoplasm and an expressed increase in the number and size of the mitochondria because the oxidative fiber diameter can be somewhat increased" (Hollman & Hettinger; Saltin & Gollnick; PDF 528-529 / p.517-518), with higher activity of "a number of mitochondrial as well as cytoplasmic enzymes." "In adaptation to work requiring endurance, hypertrophy in the muscles is not observed." As a result the muscles better "utilize pyruvate and the fatty acids," and "Endurance loads lead to an increase in the synthesis of mitochondrial proteins, to a significantly greater extent than the proteins of enzyme glycolisis and glycogenolysis (Wenger et al.,292)" (PDF 529 / p.518). "Synthesis of the mitochondrial proteins increases not only in the oxidative slow twitch muscle fibers, but also in the fast twitch fibers (Baldwin et al., 150, Yakovlev, 144)." The form of endurance that develops "is specific, corresponding to the character of the training loads (general endurance, endurance for long term work, speed and strength endurance and so on)" (Yakovlev, 137, 144; PDF 529 / p.518).

**Why it works** — Three factors, which he says "are not exclusive from one another and can be looked at as components of a single mechanism" (PDF 529-530 / p.518-519): "1. Accumulation of the recruited metabolites acting on the genetics of the cells as specific inductors of specific protein synthesis; 2. The most significant increase in degradation is of those proteins that do not appear as the decisive ones in the development of endurance; 3. The total depressed protein synthesis, on the background of which the effect of the inductors is realized and that calls forth synthesis of only proteins, is more noted in adaptation to long term muscle activity." Item 3 is garbled in translation. Inference: probably "synthesis of only certain proteins," meaning overall synthesis is held down and only the induced proteins are made. He adds that "Stronger degradation of the contractile proteins is especially expressed after long term execution of exercises for endurance" (PDF 526 / p.515), which is "one of the reasons why the strengthened adaptive protein synthesis in training for endurance does not bring about an increase in the myofibrils" (PDF 527 / p.516).

**When to apply** — Inference: when an athlete must gain aerobic capacity without gaining mass (weight-class athletes, distance athletes), or when explaining why long aerobic work does not build strength. Eric's review: "For speed-power athletes, the aerobic system's main value is inter-effort recovery (regenerating ATP between bouts), not distance capacity" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 123, Inferred (transcript)). Inference: because fast fibres also gain mitochondria by this account, aerobic work can raise the fatigue resistance of the fibres a power athlete relies on, which is consistent with that view.

**When NOT to apply** — The heart is the exception on the same page: in heart muscle there is "expressed hypertrophy." The printed sentence reads "hypertrophy in the cells of the mitochondria as a consequence of the increased size of the myofibrils" (PDF 529 / p.518). Inference: probably "the cells of the myocardium," since the sentence contrasts heart with skeletal muscle and says mitochondrial levels do not change. The claim is about adaptations from endurance training as such; it does not say mixed programmes cannot gain both. The qualifier "because the oxidative fiber diameter can be somewhat increased" (PDF 529 / p.518) sits in tension with "muscle mass and thickness of the muscle fibers ... practically does not change" (PDF 526 / p.515), so "without hypertrophy" means no general hypertrophy, not that no fibre grows at all. Literature summary with no study described and no data shown, so rated `untested`.

**Example** — Verkhoshansky's tissue survey (PDF 529 / p.518): in endurance training "stronger protein synthesis is also noted in other tissues, mainly, the heart muscle tissues," and in "the brain tissues, which includes synthesis of mitochondrial proteins (Viru, 33)."

**Related** — [[claim--training-direction-sets-which-proteins-are-synthesised-table-1]], [[claim--strength-hypertrophy-dilutes-mitochondria-and-speeds-endurance-fatigue]], [[claim--endurance-rests-on-muscle-oxidative-and-strength-qualities-not-vo2max]] (4.4, the authors' muscle-centred view of endurance), [[claim--metabolites-induce-and-hormones-amplify-adaptive-protein-synthesis]]

# Prepare Athletes for the Risky Movements Their Sport Contains Instead of Banning Them: Train Reaction, Anticipation and Falling

**What it is** — Under "Training to Avoid Injury" the authors write: "Avoidance of certain exercises which are regarded as potentially harmful may sometimes be unwise, because those very movements may occur periodically in the sport or during practice. This well-meaning approach can predispose athletes to injury since they will not have acquired the necessary involuntary motor skills to cope with higher risk actions. Therefore, it can be valuable to progressively introduce skills intended to prepare the athlete to minimise the chance of accidents and injury" (PDF 439 / p.428, checked against the page image).

**Why it works** — The authors' mechanism is skill: an athlete never exposed to a high-risk action lacks the "involuntary motor skills to cope" when the sport forces it. "Training of reactive ability can be extremely helpful in this regard, although too many athletes strengthen the body instead to achieve this end. It would be far better for them to improve speed of reaction, speed of movement, ability to anticipate impending dangers and to learn to manage dangerous events while they are happening" (PDF 439 / p.428).

**When to apply** — When a movement is dropped from a programme as "dangerous" but the sport still produces it (contact, falls, awkward landings). Introduce it "progressively." The authors' contact-sport case: "It is surprising how few rugby and American football players never learn how to fall from their colleagues in judo and wrestling, yet falling and violent bodily contact are integral parts of their games" (PDF 439 / p.428; the double negative "how few ... never" is printed so, and the sense is that few learn to fall). Eric's review: "Progressions in exercise selection, volume, and intensity are kept smooth and gradual by design; abrupt, large changes are treated as a direct injury-risk driver, not just a training-quality issue." (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 142, Inferred (transcript)). Inference: the book's "progressively introduce" matches that rule; exposure is graded, not sudden.

**When NOT to apply** — The authors say avoidance "may sometimes be unwise," not always; a movement the sport does not contain is not covered. No injury data are given. "Too many athletes strengthen the body instead" sets reactive skill against strength, but the book does not say strength work is useless for injury risk. Inference: in a rehab or novice setting, holding back a high-risk movement until basic control is present is still graded exposure, not the avoidance the authors criticise.

**Example** — The authors' own: teaching rugby and American football players the falling skills used in judo and wrestling, since falling and contact are part of their games (PDF 439 / p.428).

**Related** — [[principle--return-to-play-incomplete-until-the-athlete-perceives-full-healing]], [[heuristic--no-unsafe-stretch-only-unsafe-execution-for-individual]], [[claim--reaction-time-mostly-fixed-movement-time-trainable]], [[heuristic--progressive-and-random-segmental-training]]

**Also in 8.8** — Under "Injury Prevention by Imperfection Training" the authors widen the point from risky sport movements to imperfect execution of training movements: athletes should "cope with sub-optimal conditions by practising with imperfectly executed movements" (PDF 477 / p.466), and "religious avoidance of certain exercises can lead to an overall imbalance between muscle groups or in motor coordination" (PDF 477 / p.466). See [[heuristic--imperfection-training-practise-imperfect-execution-and-contingency-actions]] and [[framework--no-dangerous-exercises-rule-and-its-eight-qualifications]].

**Also in 8.8 (accidents, PDF 471)** — At the opening of 8.8 the authors split injury causes into accident and overtraining. Accidents "often depend on factors which lie outside the direct control of the athlete," yet "thorough physical preparation, astute situation analysis, training of reactive ability, efficient ongoing interpretation of feedback from cues provided by other players or the environment, and good anticipation can prove invaluable in minimising the risks posed by accident or unexpected events in sport" (PDF 471 / p.460, checked against the page image). See [[framework--six-fundamental-principles-of-the-injury-process]] and [[heuristic--imperfection-training-practise-imperfect-execution-and-contingency-actions]].

# When Training Load Can No Longer Rise Without Harm, Seek Supplementary Factors That Disturb Homeostasis the Way Muscular Work Does

**What it is** — The route given for Yakovlev's first task, "Finding ways of increasing the intensity of the adaptational changes in the highly trained body" (9.1 Further perspectives, PDF 561 / p.550, checked against the page image): "In resolving the first task, it appears to be rational to proceed from the level of disturbance of the biochemical homeostasis during execution of the training loads. With an increase in trainedness this disturbance decreases, and the less it becomes, the less are the following consequences remaining from the muscular activity and that lie in the base of adaptation. Because of this, with an increase in trainedness, it becomes inevitable that the training loads should increase. However, on the contemporary stage of sports development we cannot practically further increase the intensity and duration of the training loads without harming the body. A more realistic path here is to find supplementary factors that bring about disturbance of the homeostasis similar to those that are observed during muscular activity. As a result, this means strengthening the following consequent appearances, left by the latter."

**Why it works** — The first half restates 9.1 §1.5: a trained body is disturbed less by the same work, so less is left to drive adaptation (see Related). The new step is the ceiling: if load cannot rise further without harm, the extra disturbance has to come from outside the training load and add to the after-effects the training leaves.

**When to apply** — Inference: for an athlete whose volume and intensity are already at the limit, look for added stressors that act on the same systems rather than more of the same work. The page names none; candidates a reader might consider (altitude or hypoxia, heat) are the writer's examples, not the book's.

**When NOT to apply** — Rated `untested`: a reasoned proposal with no data and no named factor. Inference: the paragraph follows Yakovlev's list and reads as continued exposition of his position; the page does not mark it as Verkhoshansky's own. Inference: the "contemporary stage" is presumably elite sport at the time of writing (Yakovlev's articles are dated 1971-1976 and the paper's Fig 16 1993), and the claim that loads cannot rise further is about athletes at that ceiling, not about developing athletes, whose loads can still rise. Inference: an added stressor also adds to total stress, so it competes with recovery and with the CAR limits set out earlier in 9.1.

**Example** — The two steps as the page states them: "with an increase in trainedness, it becomes inevitable that the training loads should increase," then "we cannot practically further increase the intensity and duration of the training loads without harming the body" (PDF 561 / p.550).

**Related** — [[claim--trainedness-is-the-sum-of-session-after-effects-and-lowers-homeostatic-disturbance]] (§1.5, the smaller disturbance in a trained body), [[framework--yakovlev-three-applied-tasks-of-sports-biochemistry]], [[claim--car-volume-is-capped-and-shrinks-as-mastery-nears-the-genetic-limit]], [[claim--automatic-defence-reserve-of-about-30-percent-of-car-is-off-limits-in-natural-training]], [[claim--ldte-in-endurance-training-documented-only-after-altitude-training]], [[claim--trained-body-answers-the-same-load-with-a-smaller-hormonal-response]] (PDF 543, the same premise: the trained body answers the same work with a smaller disturbance), [[claim--strength-training-threshold-stimulus]] (the threshold rises as the athlete adapts, as in "with an increase in trainedness, it becomes inevitable that the training loads should increase," PDF 561 / p.550)

**Also in 9.1 (Further perspectives, PDF 559)** — The same pressure is named earlier as a driver of the turn to biology: "The large volume of training and competitive loads and the increasing struggle with the use of biologically active preparations have served in the latter years to increase the interest in searching for new pathways in the theory and methods of training (Verkhoshansky, 26). In doing this specialists are frequently forced to doubt and with all their power, overcome their speculative pseudo-pedagogical concepts of training and with trust, turn to the biological sciences" (PDF 559 / p.548, checked against the page image). Inference: load volume near its ceiling and the fight against doping are the two reasons he gives for looking beyond more training. See [[principle--training-theory-must-rest-on-adaptation-and-be-written-by-physiological-state-dynamics]].
